title: This page tells Google to show a different page
what: The page's canonical tag names a different address as the real one.
why: Search engines treat the page as a copy, so it may never appear in results.
fix: Give each page a canonical tag that points at its own address. Shared SEO components are the usual cause.
tech: <link rel="canonical"> on the page points at another URL

title: The feed this page advertises is broken
what: The page links to an RSS or Atom feed that returns an error (4xx or 5xx).
why: Feed readers, podcast apps and newsletter tools that follow the site stop getting new posts, usually without anyone noticing.
fix: Restore the feed at that address, or update the link rel="alternate" tag to where the feed lives now.

title: Your whole site exists at two addresses
what: Both www and the bare domain load the site, instead of one redirecting to the other.
why: Search engines can split your ranking between two copies of every page.
fix: Pick one address and 301-redirect the other to it at your host or DNS provider.
tech: the alternate host returns 200 instead of 301

title: This page asks search engines not to list it
what: The page has a robots meta tag containing noindex.
why: If that isn't on purpose, the page is invisible in search.
fix: Remove noindex from pages you want found.

title: Your robots.txt tells every search engine to stay away
what: robots.txt has a group for every crawler (User-agent: *) that disallows the whole site.
why: Search engines stop crawling the site, so new pages never appear and old ones fade out of results.
fix: Remove the Disallow: / line from the User-agent: * group, or replace it with the paths you mean to hide. This line is often left over from a staging site.
tech: robots.txt: User-agent: * with Disallow: / and no Allow that overrides it

title: Your sitemap lists pages that don't exist
what: Pages listed in the sitemap return an error (4xx or 5xx).
why: The sitemap is where you tell search engines which pages matter. Dead entries waste their visits and make them trust the sitemap less.
fix: Remove the dead addresses from the sitemap, or restore the pages. A generated sitemap usually means a deleted page is still in the CMS or the route list.

title: Google sees an almost empty page
what: Fewer than 60 words exist in the page before JavaScript runs, outside the header, nav and footer.
why: Many crawlers and AI tools read the page without running JavaScript, so they see almost nothing.
fix: Render the main content on the server. In Next.js, keep it out of client-only components and Suspense boundaries that wait for the browser.

title: The feed this page advertises is not a feed
what: The advertised feed address answers, but with something that is not RSS or Atom, often an HTML page.
why: Feed readers cannot read it, so subscribers get nothing. A framework's catch-all route is the usual cause.
fix: Serve the feed's XML at that address, or point the link rel="alternate" tag at the address that does.
tech: the feed body does not start with an XML declaration, <rss> or <feed>

title: The feed this page advertises is too large
what: The feed response is larger than 2 MB.
why: Feed readers and aggregators time out or truncate large feeds, and frameworks such as Next.js do not cache responses over 2 MB, so every request rebuilds it.
fix: Limit the feed to recent items (20 to 50 is typical) and put a summary in each item instead of the full post.
tech: the feed response is larger than 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes)

title: Your address takes several jumps to load
what: The address you entered redirects more than once before the page loads.
why: Each jump slows the first visit and can weaken how search engines credit the page.
fix: Point every redirect straight at the final address.
tech: more than one 3xx hop on the entered URL

title: Your sitemap lists pages on a different address
what: Every entry in the sitemap uses a different host than the site, for example a staging domain or the other of www and the bare domain.
why: Search engines ignore sitemap entries for a host the sitemap does not belong to, so the sitemap does nothing for this site.
fix: Generate the sitemap with the site's public address. In most frameworks this is a site URL or base URL setting.
tech: every sitemap entry's host differs from the page's host

title: Search engines can't find a list of your pages
what: There is no sitemap at /sitemap.xml, and robots.txt does not say where one is.
why: Without a sitemap, search engines find pages only by following links, so new or deep pages take longer to appear.
fix: Publish a sitemap at /sitemap.xml (most site builders and frameworks can generate one) and add a Sitemap: line with its full address to robots.txt.
tech: /sitemap.xml is not a 200 sitemap and robots.txt has no Sitemap: line

title: Your sitemap lists old addresses that redirect
what: Pages listed in the sitemap answer with a redirect (3xx) instead of the page.
why: A sitemap should list the final address of each page. Redirecting entries make search engines do extra work and can keep the old address in results.
fix: List each page at the address it redirects to. This often follows a move to https, to www, or to a new URL scheme.

title: The page doesn't say which address is the real one
why: Copies of the page with tracking parameters can be treated as separate pages.
